Non-backtracking eigenvalues and eigenvectors of random regular graphs and hypergraphs

Xiangyi Zhu Address: Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD 21218 Email address: xzhu96@jh.edu and Yizhe Zhu Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA 90007 Email address: yizhezhu@usc.edu
Date: September 25, 2026
Abstract.

The non-backtracking operator of a graph is a powerful tool in spectral graph theory and random matrix theory. Most existing results for the non-backtracking operator of a random graph concern only eigenvalues or top eigenvectors. In this paper, we take the first step in analyzing its bulk eigenvector behaviors. We demonstrate that for the non-backtracking operator BB of a random dd-regular graph, its eigenvectors corresponding to nontrivial eigenvalues are completely delocalized with high probability. Additionally, we show complete delocalization for a reduced 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n non-backtracking matrix B~\tilde{B}. By projecting all eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} onto the real line, we obtain an empirical measure that converges weakly in probability to the Kesten-McKay law for fixed d≥3d\geq 3 and to a semicircle law as d→∞d\to\infty with n→∞n\to\infty. We extend our analysis to random regular hypergraphs, including the limiting measure of the real part of the spectrum for B~\tilde{B}, ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm bounds for the eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} and BB, and a deterministic relation between eigenvectors of BB and the eigenvectors of the adjacency matrix.

As an application, we analyze the non-backtracking spectrum of the (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2})-regular stochastic block model (RSBM) and provide a spectral method based on eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} to recover the community structure exactly. We also show that there exists an isolated real eigenvalue with an informative eigenvector inside the circle of radius d1+d2−1\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1} in the spectrum of BB, analogous to the “eigenvalue insider” phenomenon previously observed for the Erdős-Rényi stochastic block model.

1. Introduction

1.1. Non-backtracking operators of random graphs

The non-backtracking operator is an important object in the study of spectral graph theory [53, 5, 8, 37, 30, 44, 36, 54]. It has recently been used as a powerful tool for studying random matrices [15, 12, 11] and for designing efficient algorithms in community detection and matrix completion [38, 15, 49, 14, 50, 51]. Many recent results on the spectrum of the non-backtracking operator have been established in various graph models, such as Erdős-Rényi graphs [56], stochastic block models [15, 22], inhomogeneous random graphs [11, 27], random regular graphs [12], and bipartite biregular graphs [18]. Very recently, some of these results have also been extended to hypergraphs [26, 50, 20]. However, so far, these results mainly focus on top eigenvalues and eigenvectors and global spectral distribution, while not much is known about bulk eigenvector behavior.

In this paper, we take a first step towards understanding the bulk eigenvectors of the non-backtracking operator in random graphs. Eigenvector delocalization is an important topic in the study of random matrices, demonstrating that many matrix models exhibit behavior similar to their Gaussian analog, a phenomenon known as universality. A unit eigenvector is considered delocalized if its infinity norm is close to that of a uniformly distributed random vector on the unit sphere up to a polylog factor. Eigenvector delocalization has been shown for many random matrix models, including non-Hermitian ones. However, for sparse and non-Hermitian models, the literature includes only a few results, such as those on eigenvector delocalization in random regular digraphs [40] and Erdős-Rényi digraphs [33] with growing average degrees.

The non-backtracking operator BB for a random dd-regular graph is a sparse and non-Hermitian operator, where each row and column of BB has exactly (d−1)(d-1) nonzero entries. It can also be viewed as the adjacency matrix of a random (d−1)(d-1)-regular digraph with (n​d)(nd) vertices. However, not all (d−1)(d-1)-regular digraphs can be obtained in this way (see [44, Theorem 2.3]), and the eigenvalue distribution of BB is very different from the conjectured oriented Kesten-McKay law for a uniformly chosen random (d−1)(d-1)-regular digraph [13]. A simulation of the non-backtracking spectrum of a random dd-regular graph is shown in Figure 1.

In Theorem 3.3, we show that with high probability, all eigenvectors corresponding to nontrivial non-backtracking eigenvalues are completely delocalized. The main idea behind the proof is to use the delocalization [35] and spectral gap [35, 12] results for the adjacency matrix of a random dd-regular graph to understand eigenvector delocalization for the non-backtracking matrix with the help of the Ihara-Bass formula [8]. The algebraic structure of the non-backtracking operator enables the translation of eigenvalue and eigenvector information from the corresponding adjacency matrix. However, this precise algebraic connection between these two operators is only available for regular graphs. Exploring beyond dd-regular graphs is an interesting future direction. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first random directed graph model with bounded degree for which eigenvector delocalization has been established.

In the course of proving non-backtracking eigenvector delocalization, we show in Theorem 3.1 the convergence in probability to the Kesten-McKay law and semicircle law for fixed dd and growing dd when projecting the eigenvalues of the non-backtracking operator onto the real line. From the Ihara-Bass formula, another 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n non-Hermitian block matrix B~\tilde{B} closely related to BB emerges, which we call a reduced non-backtracking operator [5, 56, 22, 48]. We also demonstrate that the eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} are completely delocalized with high probability in Theorem 3.2.

1.2. Extension to regular hypergraphs

The spectral theory for hypergraphs has drawn considerable interest due to its applications in number theory, community detection, and network analysis [28, 39, 47, 52]. In [6, 50, 20], spectral algorithms based on the non-backtracking eigenvectors were studied for community detection problems in hypergraph stochastic block models. Several results we obtained for random regular graphs can be generalized to random regular hypergraphs, which is a popular hypergraph model studied in combinatorics, statistical physics, and computer science [21, 26, 31, 19, 46].

In Theorem 3.7, we show that by projecting the eigenvalues of a non-backtracking operator BB for random regular hypergraphs, we can obtain different limiting measures depending on the regime of d,kd,k. We provide an exact spectral relation between a reduced non-backtracking operator B~\tilde{B} and the adjacency matrix AA of a regular hypergraph in Lemma  7.1. A precise relation between eigenvectors of BB and AA is given in Lemma 8.1, which generalizes the result for regular graphs in [41]. These relations are used to show ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm bounds on eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} and BB in Theorem 3.8.

1.3. Application in a regular stochastic block model

Community detection in the stochastic block model is an important topic in statistical physics, machine learning, and network science [1]. Using the non-backtracking operator to detect the community structure is proven to achieve the information-theoretical threshold in many settings [15, 50]. However, the spectrum of the non-backtracking operator for stochastic block models is not fully understood. An intriguing behavior of the spectrum for the non-backtracking matrix BB in the Erdős-Rényi stochastic block model with constant expected degree was observed in [23], namely, that there exists a real eigenvalue inside the bulk spectrum of BB close to the ratio of the top two eigenvalues of BB. This was justified in [22] in the dense regime when the expected degree is ω⁡(log⁡n)\omega(\log n). We study an analog of the stochastic block model in the random regular graph setting, which is called the regular stochastic block model (RSBM) [17, 7, 45] studied in the literature, which exhibits different behaviors from the Erdős-Rényi stochastic block model (SBM). The RSBM is constructed by combining a random d2d_{2}-regular bipartite graph and a random d1d_{1}-regular graph; see Definition 3.9 for a precise description.

We confirm the eigenvalue insider phenomenon in the RSBM in Theorem 3.10 and Corollary 3.11: When (d1−d2)2>4​(d1+d2−1)(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}>4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1), a real eigenvalue of B~\tilde{B} exists inside the circle of radius d1+d2−1\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}, and the corresponding eigenvector reveals the community structure exactly. For the two-community Erdős-Rényi SBM, weak recovery is information-theoretically impossible below the Kesten–Stigum threshold [43]. By contrast, in the RSBM, the community assignment vector σ\sigma is an exact adjacency eigenvector with eigenvalue d1−d2d_{1}-d_{2}. Based on this algebraic structure and numerical evidence, Barucca [7] conjectured that the planted partition admits efficient exact recovery whenever d1>d2>0d_{1}>d_{2}>0; to the best of our knowledge, this conjecture remains open in the full parameter regime.

Organization of the paper

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide some basic notation and definitions for regular graphs, the non-backtracking operator, and hypergraphs. In Section 3, we state the main results for random regular graphs, random regular hypergraphs, and the regular stochastic block model, respectively. Sections 4 to 9 contain all the proofs. In Section 10, we discuss the open problem of generalizing the results to Erdős-Rényi graphs.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Regular graphs

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph. GG is dd-regular of size nn if each vertex has degree dd and |V|=n|V|=n. For given nn and dd, we say GG is a random dd-regular graph if it is uniformly chosen from all dd-regular graphs with nn vertices.

The (i,j)(i,j)-th entry of the adjacency matrix AA of a graph GG is defined as

Ai​j={1if ​{i,j}∈E,0otherwise.A_{ij}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\{i,j\}\in E,\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

The degree matrix DD of a graph GG is a diagonal matrix where Di​i=∑j∈VAi​jD_{ii}=\sum_{j\in V}A_{ij}. Define the oriented edge set E→\vec{E} for GG as

E→={(i,j):{i,j}∈E}.\displaystyle\vec{E}=\{(i,j):\{i,j\}\in E\}. (1)

Each edge yields two oriented edges; therefore, |E→|=2​|E||\vec{E}|=2|E|.

Definition 2.1 (Non-backtracking operator).

The non-backtracking operator BB of GG is a non-Hermitian operator of size |E→|×|E→||\vec{E}|\times|\vec{E}|. For any (u,v),(x,y)∈E→(u,v),(x,y)\in\vec{E}, BB is defined as

B(u,v),(x,y)={1v=x, u≠y,0otherwise.B_{(u,v),(x,y)}=\begin{cases}1&\text{$v=x$, $u\neq y$},\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

In particular, for a dd-regular graph with nn vertices, the corresponding BB is of size n​d×n​dnd\times nd. A useful identity we will use in this paper is the following Ihara-Bass formula [8].

Lemma 2.2 (Ihara-Bass formula).

For any graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), and any z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, the following identity holds:

det(B−z​I)=(z2−1)|E|−n​det(z2​I−z​A+D−I).\displaystyle\det(B-zI)=(z^{2}-1)^{|E|-n}\det(z^{2}I-zA+D-I). (2)

Define a block matrix

B~=[0D−I−IA]∈ℝ2​n×2​n.\displaystyle\tilde{B}=\begin{bmatrix}0&D-I\\ -I&A\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}. (3)

Then from (2), we have

det(B−z​I)=(z2−1)|E|−n​det(B~−z​I).\displaystyle\det(B-zI)=(z^{2}-1)^{|E|-n}\det(\tilde{B}-zI). (4)

The identity (4) implies that BB and B~\tilde{B} share the same spectrum, up to the multiplicity of trivial eigenvalues ±1\pm 1. We also call B~\tilde{B} the reduced non-backtracking matrix of GG. When GG is a dd-regular graph with nn vertices, (2) can be further simplified to

det(B−z​I)=(z2−1)n​d/2−n​det(z2​I−z​A+(d−1)​I).\displaystyle\det(B-zI)=(z^{2}-1)^{nd/2-n}\det(z^{2}I-zA+(d-1)I). (5)

2.2. Regular hypergraphs

In this section, we include some standard definitions of hypergraphs.

Definition 2.3 (Hypergraph).

A hypergraph HH consists of a set VV of vertices and a set EE of hyperedges such that each hyperedge is a nonempty set of VV. A hypergraph HH is kk-uniform for an integer k≥2k\geq 2 if every hyperedge e∈Ee\in E contains exactly kk vertices. The degree of ii, denoted deg⁡(i)\deg(i), is the number of all hyperedges incident to ii.

A hypergraph is dd-regular if all of its vertices have degree dd. A hypergraph is (d,k)(d,k)-regular if it is both dd-regular and kk-uniform. See Figure 2 for an example.

Definition 2.4 (Adjacency matrix of a hypergraph).

For a hypergraph HH with nn vertices, we associate a n×nn\times n symmetric matrix AA called the adjacency matrix of HH. For i≠ji\not=j, we define Ai​jA_{ij} as the number of hyperedges containing both ii and jj; we define Ai​i=0A_{ii}=0 for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. When the hypergraph is 22-uniform, this is the definition for the adjacency matrix of a graph.

3. Main results

3.1. Random regular graphs

Let μ1,…,μ2​n\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{2n} be the eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B}. Define xix_{i} to be the real part of μi\mu_{i}. The empirical measure of {xi,1≤i≤2n}\{x_{i},1\leq i\leq 2n\} is denoted as

μ=12​n​∑i=12​nδxi.\mu=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{2n}\delta_{x_{i}}.

The following theorem characterizes the eigenvalue distribution of B~\tilde{B} after projecting all eigenvalues to the real line.

Theorem 3.1 (Projecting eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} to the real line).

The following holds for the reduced non-backtracking matrix B~\tilde{B} of a uniformly chosen random dd-regular graph:

  1. (1)

    When d≥3d\geq 3 is a fixed integer, μ\mu converges weakly in probability to a rescaled Kesten-McKay distribution μKM\mu_{\mathrm{KM}} supported on [−d−1,d−1][-\sqrt{d-1},\sqrt{d-1}], where

    μKM(x)=2​d​(d−1)−x2π⁡(d2−4​x2)𝟏{|x|≤d−1}.\mu_{\mathrm{KM}}(x)=\frac{2d\sqrt{(d-1)-x^{2}}}{\pi(d^{2}-4x^{2})}~\mathbf{1}\left\{|x|\leq\sqrt{d-1}\right\}.
  2. (2)

    When d→∞d\to\infty as n→∞n\to\infty, the empirical measure of {2​xid−1,i∈[2​n]}\left\{\frac{2x_{i}}{\sqrt{d-1}},i\in[2n]\right\} converges weakly in probability to a semicircle law μSC\mu_{\mathrm{SC}}, where

    μSC(x)=12​π4−x2𝟏{|x|≤2}.\displaystyle\mu_{\mathrm{SC}}(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^{2}}~\mathbf{1}\{|x|\leq 2\}. (6)

Figure 3 is a simulation for the projected eigenvalues on the real line of a random regular graph. Similar results have been established for Erdős-Rényi graphs G⁡(n,p)G(n,p) with n​p=ω⁡(log⁡n)np=\omega(\log n) [56] and for stochastic block models [22] in the same regime.

We now move on to study the eigenvectors of BB and B~\tilde{B}. Note that each unit eigenvector of B~\tilde{B} is in ℂ2​n\mathbb{C}^{2n}. We show they are completely delocalized based on the eigenvector delocalization results in [35] for the adjacency matrix of a random dd-regular graph.

Theorem 3.2 (Eigenvector delocalization for B~\tilde{B}).

Let d≥3d\geq 3 be fixed, and B~\tilde{B} be the reduced non-backtracking matrix of a random dd-regular graph. Let uiu_{i} for i∈[2​n]i\in[2n] be the ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized eigenvector associated with μi\mu_{i}. Then there exist absolute constants C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 such that with probability at least 1−n−C11-n^{-C_{1}}, for all i∈[2​n]i\in[2n],

‖ui‖∞≤logC2⁡(n)n.\displaystyle\|u_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\log^{C_{2}}(n)}{\sqrt{n}}. (7)

By a different argument with the help of the Ihara-Bass formula, we can also show that unit eigenvectors of BB as a vector in ℂn​d\mathbb{C}^{nd} are completely delocalized.

Theorem 3.3 (Eigenvector delocalization for BB).

Let d≥3d\geq 3 be fixed, and BB be the non-backtracking matrix of a random dd-regular graph. Let μi\mu_{i} for i∈[2​n]i\in[2n] be the eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B}. Then there exist absolute constants C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 such that with probability at least 1−n−C11-n^{-C_{1}}, all the unit eigenvectors wiw_{i} of BB associated with μi≠±1\mu_{i}\not=\pm 1 satisfy

‖wi‖∞≤logC2⁡(n)n​d.\displaystyle\|w_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\log^{C_{2}}(n)}{\sqrt{nd}}. (8)

The ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norms of eigenvectors of BB and B~\tilde{B} are illustrated in Figure 4. Similar results for non-backtracking eigenvectors of random dd-regular graphs for growing dd can be proved in the same way by using the eigenvector delocalization bounds for the adjacency matrix in [24, 55, 10, 9].

Remark 3.4 (Eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues ±1\pm 1 in Equation (5)).

In Equation (5), we see there are trivial eigenvalues ±1\pm 1 of BB with an extra multiplicity n​d2−n\frac{nd}{2}-n which are not given by eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B}. The structure of the eigenspaces of ±1\pm 1 was discussed in [41, Proof of Proposition 3.1].

3.2. Random regular hypergraphs

Definition 3.5 (Non-backtracking operator of a hypergraph).

For a hypergraph H=(V,E)H=(V,E), its non-backtracking operator BB is a square matrix indexed by oriented hyperedges

E→={(i,e):i∈V,e∈E,i∈e}\vec{E}=\{(i,e):i\in V,e\in E,i\in e\}

with entries given by

B(i,e),(j,f)={1if j∈e∖{i},f≠e,0otherwise,B_{(i,e),(j,f)}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $j\in e\setminus\{i\},f\not=e$,}\\ 0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}

for any oriented hyperedges (i,e),(j,f)∈E→(i,e),(j,f)\in\vec{E}.

This is a generalization of the graph non-backtracking operators to hypergraphs. For a kk-uniform hypergraph H=(V,E)H=(V,E), define the 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n reduced non-backtracking matrix B~\tilde{B} as

B~=(0(D−I)−(k−1)​IA−(k−2)​I),\tilde{B}=\begin{pmatrix}0&(D-I)\\ -(k-1)I&A-(k-2)I\end{pmatrix}, (9)

where AA is the adjacency matrix of HH, and DD is the diagonal degree matrix with

Di​i=#⁡{e∈E:i∈e}.\displaystyle D_{ii}=\#\{e\in E:i\in e\}. (10)

The following Ihara-Bass formula for hypergraphs was proved in [50]. Lemma 3.6 shows that the spectrum of B~\tilde{B} is identical to that of BB, except for possible trivial eigenvalues at 1{1} and −(k−1)-(k-1).

Lemma 3.6 (Lemma 1 in [50]).

Let H=(V,E)H=(V,E) be a kk-uniform hypergraph. The following identity holds for any z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}:

det(B−z​I)\displaystyle\det(B-zI)
=(z−1)(k−1)​|E|−n​(z+(k−1))|E|−n​det(z2+(k−2)​z−z​A+(k−1)​(D−I))\displaystyle=(z-1)^{(k-1)|E|-n}(z+(k-1))^{|E|-n}\det\left(z^{2}+(k-2)z-zA+(k-1)(D-I)\right)

Theorem 3.8 shows that eigenvector delocalization of AA implies eigenvector delocalization for BB and B~\tilde{B}. However, no eigenvector delocalization results are available in the literature for the adjacency matrix random regular hypergraphs. It’s possible that by adapting the result of eigenvector delocalization for bipartite biregular graphs [57, Corollary 2.8] together with the connection between random regular hypergraphs and random bipartite biregular graphs established in [26], one can obtain an eigenvector delocalization bound for the adjacency matrix in the random regular hypergraph case.

3.3. Community detection in the RSBM

Definition 3.9 (Regular stochastic block model (RSBM)).

For an even integer nn and two integers d1d_{1} and d2d_{2}, the regular stochastic block model with vertex set [n][n] is obtained as follows. Choose a partition V1,V2V_{1},V_{2} of equal size n/2n/2 of the vertex set [n][n], uniformly from among the set of all such partitions. Choose two independent copies of uniform d1d_{1}-regular graphs with vertex set V1V_{1}, respectively V2V_{2}. Finally, connect the vertices from V1V_{1} with those from V2V_{2} by a uniformly random d2d_{2}-bipartite regular graph.

Let σ∈{−1,1}n\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^{n} be a vector for the community assignment defined by

σi={1i∈V1−1i∈V2.\displaystyle\sigma_{i}=\begin{cases}1&i\in V_{1}\\ -1&i\in V_{2}.\end{cases} (15)

The community detection problem for the regular stochastic block model is to observe a random graph sampled from the model and construct an estimator for the community assignment vector σ\sigma.

Note that a graph sampled from this model is a random (d1+d2)(d_{1}+d_{2})-regular graph but not uniformly distributed. It has been shown in [16, Proposition 1] that the RSBM is asymptotically distinguishable from a uniformly chosen random regular graph with the same degree. However, some of our results for deterministic regular graphs can still be applied to this model. We describe the real eigenvalues and eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} as follows:

Theorem 3.10 (Real eigenvalues and eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B}).

Let B~\tilde{B} be the reduced non-backtracking operator of an (n,d1,d2)(n,d_{1},d_{2})-regular stochastic block model. Then, the following holds:

  1. (1)

    d1+d2−1d_{1}+d_{2}-1 is an eigenvalue of B~\tilde{B} with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1,…,1]⊤∈ℝ2​nv_{1}=\left[1,\dots,1\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n} and 11 is an eigenvalue of B~\tilde{B} with the corresponding eigenvector

    v1′=[1,…,1,1d1+d2−1,…,1d1+d2−1]⊤∈ℝ2​n.v_{1}^{\prime}=\left[1,\dots,1,\frac{1}{d_{1}+d_{2}-1},\dots,\frac{1}{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}.
  2. (2)

    When (d1−d2)2>4​(d1+d2−1)(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}>4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1), there are two real eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} given by

    μ2,μ2′=d1−d2±(d1−d2)2−4​(d1+d2−1)2,\displaystyle\mu_{2},\mu_{2}^{\prime}=\frac{d_{1}-d_{2}\pm\sqrt{(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}-4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1)}}{2}, (16)

    with the corresponding eigenvector

    v2=[σμ2d1+d2−1​σ],v2′=[σμ2′d1+d2−1​σ].\displaystyle v_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma\\ \frac{\mu_{2}}{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}\sigma\end{bmatrix},\quad v_{2}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma\\ \frac{\mu_{2}^{\prime}}{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}\sigma\end{bmatrix}. (17)
  3. (3)

    When (d1−d2)2>4​(d1+d2−1)(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}>4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1) and d1d_{1} is even, with high probability, the four values d1+d2−1,1,μ2d_{1}+d_{2}-1,1,\mu_{2} and μ2′\mu_{2}^{\prime} are real eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} with multiplicity one, and the rest of the eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} are within o⁡(1)o(1) distance from the circle of radius d1+d2−1\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}.

See Figure 5 for a simulation on the spectrum of an RSBM and an Erdős-Rényi SBM. From Theorem 3.10, we obtain the following corollary for exact recovery with a spectral method in the RSBM.

Corollary 3.11 (Exact recovery in the RSBM).

Assume (d1−d2)2>4​(d1+d2−1)(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}>4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1) and d1d_{1} is even. Let u2=[x2y2],u2′=[x2′y2′]u_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{2}\\ y_{2}\end{bmatrix},u_{2}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{2}^{\prime}\\ y_{2}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix} be eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} corresponding to eigenvalue μ2\mu_{2} and μ2′\mu_{2}^{\prime}, respectively. Then, with high probability, each of the four vectors x2,y2,x2′,y2′x_{2},y_{2},x_{2}^{\prime},y_{2}^{\prime} is a scalar multiple of the community assignment vector σ\sigma, namely, x2,y2,x2′,y2′∈span⁡{σ}x_{2},y_{2},x_{2}^{\prime},y_{2}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{span}\{\sigma\}.

Corollary 3.11 implies that both eigenvectors u2u_{2} and u2′u_{2}^{\prime} of B~\tilde{B} can exactly recover the community assignment vector σ\sigma with high probability. Such a spectral method based on the eigenvector associated with the insider eigenvalue for the Erdős-Rényi SBM was conjectured in [23] and remains open. Compared with the regular stochastic block model, the key difference for the Erdős-Rényi stochastic block model is the lack of degree concentration in the very sparse regime, which makes it challenging to establish a direct connection between eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} and AA.

Remark 3.12 (The parity constraint of d1d_{1}).

In Theorem 3.10, the constraint that d1d_{1} is even is a technical condition due to the proof technique in [16], which involves random lifts studied in [12, 29]. It was conjectured in [16] that such a restriction can be removed. We expect by adapting the proof techniques in [12, 18], Theorem 3.10 can be shown for all (d1−d2)2>4​(d1+d2−1)(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}>4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1). We leave it as a future direction.

4. Proof of Theorem 3.1

We first derive an algebraic relation between eigenvalues and eigenvectors of AA and BB when GG is a dd-regular graph, from which the known spectral laws for AA give the limiting distribution of the real parts of the eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B}.

Lemma 4.1 (Spectral relation between AA and B~\tilde{B}).

Let GG be a dd-regular graph with adjacency matrix AA and non-backtracking matrix BB and d≥2d\geq 2. Let viv_{i} be an eigenvector of AA corresponding to eigenvalue λi\lambda_{i} for i∈[n]i\in[n]. Then

μi,μi′=λi±λi2−4​(d−1)2\mu_{i},\mu_{i}^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda_{i}\pm\sqrt{{\lambda_{i}}^{2}-4(d-1)}}{2} (18)

are two eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B}, with two corresponding eigenvectors of the form

ui=[viμid−1​vi],ui′=[viμi′d−1​vi].u_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}\\ \frac{\mu_{i}}{d-1}v_{i}\end{bmatrix},\quad u_{i}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}\\ \frac{\mu_{i}^{\prime}}{d-1}v_{i}\end{bmatrix}. (19)
Proof.

Let [xy]\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix} for x,y∈ℂnx,y\in\mathbb{C}^{n} be an eigenvector of B~\tilde{B} with respect to an eigenvalue μ\mu. Then we have

μ​[xy]=[0(d−1)​I−IA]​[xy].\mu\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&(d-1)I\\ -I&A\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}.

This equation implies

y=μd−1​x,A​x=(μ+d−1μ)​x.\displaystyle y=\frac{\mu}{d-1}x,\quad Ax=\left(\mu+\frac{d-1}{\mu}\right)x. (20)

For each eigenvalue λi\lambda_{i} of AA with a corresponding eigenvector vi∈ℝnv_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, there are two corresponding eigenvalues μi,μi′\mu_{i},\mu^{\prime}_{i} of B~\tilde{B} satisfying the quadratic equation

x2−λi​x+d−1=0.x^{2}-\lambda_{i}x+d-1=0. (21)

In particular, λ1=d\lambda_{1}=d gives two real eigenvalues μ1=d−1\mu_{1}=d-1 and μ1′=1\mu_{1}^{\prime}=1.

By counting multiplicity, Equation (21) gives all the 2​n2n eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B}. Thus, by Equations (20) and  (21), there are nn eigenvectors of B~\tilde{B} of the form

ui=[viμid−1​vi]​, where ​μi=λi+λi2−4​(d−1)2,u_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}\\ \frac{\mu_{i}}{d-1}v_{i}\end{bmatrix}\text{, where }\mu_{i}=\frac{\lambda_{i}+\sqrt{{\lambda_{i}}^{2}-4(d-1)}}{2}, (22)

and other nn eigenvectors of the form,

ui′=[viμi′d−1​vi]​, where ​μi′=λi−λi2−4​(d−1)2.u_{i}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}\\ \frac{\mu_{i}^{\prime}}{d-1}v_{i}\end{bmatrix}\text{, where }\mu_{i}^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda_{i}-\sqrt{{\lambda_{i}}^{2}-4(d-1)}}{2}. (23)

∎

With Lemma 4.1, we are ready to prove Theorem 3.1 for random dd-regular graphs.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

From Equation (21), when |λi|2≤4​(d−1)|\lambda_{i}|^{2}\leq 4(d-1), we have

μi+μi′=λi,|μi|=|μi′|=d−1,\mu_{i}+\mu_{i}^{\prime}=\lambda_{i},\quad|\mu_{i}|=|\mu_{i}^{\prime}|=\sqrt{d-1},

and the real parts of μi,μi′\mu_{i},\mu_{i}^{\prime} satisfy

xi=xi′=λi2.\displaystyle x_{i}=x_{i}^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda_{i}}{2}. (24)

The Kesten-McKay law in [42] shows that with high probability, the limiting eigenvalue distribution of the adjacency matrix for a random dd-regular graph converges weakly to a probability measure with density

f(x)=d​4​(d−1)−x22​π​(d2−x2)𝟏{|x|≤2d−1}.f(x)=\frac{d\sqrt{4(d-1)-x^{2}}}{2\pi(d^{2}-x^{2})}\mathbf{1}\left\{|x|\leq 2\sqrt{d-1}\right\}.

From the Kesten-McKay law above, with high probability, there are n−o⁡(n)n-o(n) eigenvalues λi\lambda_{i} that satisfy |λi|2≤4​(d−1)|\lambda_{i}|^{2}\leq 4(d-1). Therefore, with high probability, there are 2​n−o⁡(n)2n-o(n) eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} inside the circle of radius d−1\sqrt{d-1}, and nn pairs of xi,xi′x_{i},x_{i}^{\prime} satisfy (24). Therefore, the empirical measure of the real parts of μi\mu_{i} converges weakly in probability to a rescaled Kesten-McKay law given by

μKM(x)=2​d​(d−1)−x2π⁡(d2−4​x2)𝟏{|x|≤d−1}.\mu_{\mathrm{KM}}(x)=\frac{2d\sqrt{(d-1)-x^{2}}}{\pi(d^{2}-4x^{2})}\mathbf{1}\left\{|x|\leq\sqrt{d-1}\right\}. (25)

Recall that AA is the adjacency matrix for a random dd-regular graph on nn vertices; when d→∞d\to\infty as n→∞n\to\infty, it is shown in [55, 24] that the empirical spectral distribution of Ad−1\frac{A}{\sqrt{d-1}} converges weakly in probability to a semicircle law. With Equation (24), following the same argument as in the case for fixed dd, the empirical measure 12​n​∑i=12​nδ2​xi/d−1\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{2n}\delta_{2x_{i}/\sqrt{d-1}} converges weakly in probability to the semicircle law. ∎

Lemma 5.1 (Theorem 1.4 in [35]).

Let AA be the adjacency matrix of a dd-regular graph. Then, for any fixed d≥3d\geq 3, there exists absolute constants C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 such that with probability at least 1−n−C11-n^{-C_{1}}, all unit eigenvectors viv_{i} of AA satisfy

‖vi‖∞≤logC2⁡(n)n.\displaystyle\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\log^{C_{2}}(n)}{\sqrt{n}}. (26)

From (19), any eigenvector uiu_{i} of B~\tilde{B} associated with viv_{i} of AA satisfies

‖ui‖∞‖ui‖2≤max⁡{1,|μi|d−1}1+|μi|2(d−1)2​‖vi‖∞‖vi‖2≤‖vi‖∞‖vi‖2.\displaystyle\frac{\|u_{i}\|_{\infty}}{\|u_{i}\|_{2}}\leq\frac{\max\left\{1,\frac{|\mu_{i}|}{d-1}\right\}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{|\mu_{i}|^{2}}{(d-1)^{2}}}}\frac{\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}}{\|v_{i}\|_{2}}\leq\frac{\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}}{\|v_{i}\|_{2}}. (27)

7. Proof of Theorem 3.7

Similar to Section 4, we first establish a spectral relation between AA and B~\tilde{B} for a regular hypergraph and apply the limiting spectral distribution of AA to B~\tilde{B} in the three regimes of (d,k)(d,k).

Lemma 7.1 (Spectral relation between AA and B~\tilde{B}).

Let H=(V,E)H=(V,E) be a kk-uniform, dd-regular hypergraph with adjacency matrix AA and reduced non-backtracking matrix B~\tilde{B}. Let λi\lambda_{i} be an eigenvalue of AA. Then each λi\lambda_{i} corresponds to two eigenvalues μi,μi′\mu_{i},\mu_{i}^{\prime} of B~\tilde{B}, which satisfy the equation

μ2−(λi−k+2)​μ+(d−1)​(k−1)=0,\mu^{2}-(\lambda_{i}-k+2)\mu+(d-1)(k-1)=0, (51)

and which have corresponding eigenvectors

ui=[viμid−1​vi],ui′=[viμi′d−1​vi].u_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}\\ \frac{\mu_{i}}{d-1}v_{i}\end{bmatrix},\quad u_{i}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}\\ \frac{\mu_{i}^{\prime}}{d-1}v_{i}\end{bmatrix}. (52)
Proof.

Let [xy]\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix} for x,y∈ℂnx,y\in\mathbb{C}^{n} be an eigenvector of B~\tilde{B} with respect to an eigenvalue μ\mu, we have

μ​[xy]=[0(d−1)​I−(k−1)​IA−(k−2)​I]​[xy].\mu\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&(d-1)I\\ -(k-1)I&A-(k-2)I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}.

This equation implies

Proof of Theorem 3.7.

With the relation (55), we can follow the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 3.1 to complete the proof of Theorem 3.7. ∎

8. Proof of Theorem 3.8

In this section, we derive the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm bounds for B~\widetilde{B} and BB separately using their eigenvector relations with AA. By Lemma 7.1, the bound for B~\widetilde{B} follows directly from (52).

Proof of Theorem 3.8 (1).

From (52), the corresponding unit eigenvectors ui,ui′u_{i},u_{i}^{\prime} satisfy

‖ui‖∞,‖ui′‖∞=max⁡{1,|μi|d−1}1+|μi|2(d−1)2​‖vi‖∞≤‖vi‖∞.\|u_{i}\|_{\infty},\|u_{i}^{\prime}\|_{\infty}=\frac{\max\left\{1,\frac{|\mu_{i}|}{d-1}\right\}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{|\mu_{i}|^{2}}{(d-1)^{2}}}}\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}.

This proves the first statement of Theorem 3.8. ∎

We now consider the second statement of Theorem 3.8. The following lemma provides a relation between eigenvectors of BB and AA for regular hypergraphs.

Lemma 8.1 (Eigenvectors of BB for regular hypergraphs).

If w~i,w~i′≠0\tilde{w}_{i},\tilde{w}_{i}^{\prime}\not=0, then each of w~i,w~i′\tilde{w}_{i},\tilde{w}_{i}^{\prime} is an eigenvector of BB associated with μi,μi′\mu_{i},\mu_{i}^{\prime}, respectively.

=μi(∑(y,f)∈E→:y∈e,y≠x,f≠e∑z∈f,z≠yvi(z))−(d−1)(k−1)∑y∈e,y≠xvi(y)\displaystyle=\mu_{i}\left(\sum_{(y,f)\in\vec{E}:y\in e,y\not=x,f\not=e}\sum_{z\in f,z\not=y}v_{i}(z)\right)-(d-1)(k-1)\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y) (62)
=μi​(∑y∈e,y≠x(A​vi)​(y)−∑y∈e,y≠x∑z∈e,z≠yvi​(z))−(d−1)​(k−1)​∑y∈e,y≠xvi​(y)\displaystyle=\mu_{i}\left(\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}(Av_{i})(y)-\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}\sum_{z\in e,z\not=y}v_{i}(z)\right)-(d-1)(k-1)\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y) (63)

−(d−1)(k−1)∑y∈e,y≠xvi(y)\displaystyle\quad-(d-1)(k-1)\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y) (65)
=(μi​λi−(k−2)​μi−(d−1)​(k−1))​(∑y∈e,y≠xvi​(y))−μi​(k−1)​vi​(x)\displaystyle=(\mu_{i}\lambda_{i}-(k-2)\mu_{i}-(d-1)(k-1))\left(\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y)\right)-\mu_{i}(k-1)v_{i}(x) (66)

Lemma 8.1 can be used to prove the following deterministic ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm bound for eigenvectors. When k=2k=2, Lemma 8.2 reduces to Lemma 6.2.

Lemma 8.2 (Deterministic ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm bound for eigenvectors of BB).

Let BB be the non-backtracking operator of a (d,k)(d,k)-regular hypergraph. Let w~i\tilde{w}_{i} be the eigenvector of BB associated with μi\mu_{i} constructed in Lemma 8.1 with μi∉{1,(d−1)​(k−1)}\mu_{i}\not\in\{1,(d-1)(k-1)\} and λi\lambda_{i} be the corresponding eigenvalue of AA. Then

⋅(μi′​(∑y∈e,y≠xvi​(y))−(k−1)​vi​(x))\displaystyle\quad\cdot\left(\mu_{i}^{\prime}\bigg(\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y)\bigg)-(k-1)v_{i}(x)\right) (72)
=|μi|2​∑(x,e)∈E→(∑y∈e,y≠xvi​(y))2+(k−1)2​∑(x,e)∈E→vi​(x)2\displaystyle=|\mu_{i}|^{2}\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}\bigg(\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y)\bigg)^{2}+(k-1)^{2}\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}v_{i}(x)^{2} (73)
−(μi+μi′)(k−1)∑(x,e)∈E→(∑y∈e,y≠xvi(y))vi(x)\displaystyle\quad-(\mu_{i}+\mu_{i}^{\prime})(k-1)\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}\bigg(\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y)\bigg)v_{i}(x) (74)
=(d−1)​(k−1)​∑(x,e)∈E→(∑y∈e,y≠xvi​(y))2+(k−1)2​∑(x,e)∈E→vi​(x)2\displaystyle=(d-1)(k-1)\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}\bigg(\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y)\bigg)^{2}+(k-1)^{2}\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}v_{i}(x)^{2} (75)
−(λi−k+2)∑(x,e)∈E→(∑y∈e,y≠xvi(y))vi(x).\displaystyle\quad-(\lambda_{i}-k+2)\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}\bigg(\sum_{y\in e,y\not=x}v_{i}(y)\bigg)v_{i}(x). (76)

For the first term in (76),

=\displaystyle= ∑(x,e)∈E→(∑y∈evi​(y))2−2​∑(x,e)∈E→(∑y∈evi​(y))​vi​(x)+∑(x,e)∈E→vi​(x)2.\displaystyle\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}\bigg(\sum_{y\in e}v_{i}(y)\bigg)^{2}-2\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}\bigg(\sum_{y\in e}v_{i}(y)\bigg)v_{i}(x)+\sum_{(x,e)\in\vec{E}}v_{i}(x)^{2}. (78)

With Lemma 8.2, we are ready to prove the second statement of Theorem 3.8.

Proof of Theorem 3.8 (2).

Let AA be the adjacency matrix of a (d,k)(d,k)-random regular hypergraph. The largest eigenvalue of AA is d⁡(k−1)d(k-1) with an eigenvector v1=1n​[1,…,1]⊤v_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}[1,\dots,1]^{\top}. ‖w~1‖∞‖w~1‖2=1n​d=1d​‖vi‖∞.\displaystyle\frac{\|\tilde{w}_{1}\|_{\infty}}{\|\tilde{w}_{1}\|_{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{nd}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}. (86)

−2​(k−1)​(d−1)+k−2−εn≤λ≤2​(k−1)​(d−1)+k−2+εn,-2\sqrt{(k-1)(d-1)}+k-2-\varepsilon_{n}\leq\lambda\leq 2\sqrt{(k-1)(d-1)}+k-2+\varepsilon_{n}, (87)

asymptotically almost surely with εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0 as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. With (87) and (85), we have, with high probability,

‖w~i‖22\displaystyle\|\tilde{w}_{i}\|_{2}^{2} ≥(k−1)​(d−1−k−1)2​((k−1)​(d−1)+1)2+o⁡(1).\displaystyle\geq(k-1)(\sqrt{d-1}-\sqrt{k-1})^{2}(\sqrt{(k-1)(d-1)}+1)^{2}+o(1). (88)

By the spectral gap bound for any eigenvalues μ≠(d−1)​(k−1)\mu\neq(d-1)(k-1) of BB from [26, Theorem 5.5], we have

|μ|≤(k−1)​(d−1)+o⁡(1)|\mu|\leq\sqrt{(k-1)(d-1)}+o(1) (89)

with high probability. Applying Lemma 8.2, together with (88) and (89), we have, for d>k≥3d>k\geq 3, with high probability,

‖w~i‖∞‖w~i‖2\displaystyle\frac{\|\tilde{w}_{i}\|_{\infty}}{\|\tilde{w}_{i}\|_{2}} ≤((k−1)​(d−1)+1)​k−1+o⁡(1)(d−1−k−1)​((k−1)​(d−1)+1)​‖vi‖∞\displaystyle\leq\frac{(\sqrt{(k-1)(d-1)}+1)\sqrt{k-1}+o(1)}{\big(\sqrt{d-1}-\sqrt{k-1}\big)\big(\sqrt{(k-1)(d-1)}+1\big)}\|v_{i}\|_{\infty} (90)
≤k−1+o⁡(1)d−1−k−1​‖vi‖∞.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sqrt{k-1}+o(1)}{\sqrt{d-1}-\sqrt{k-1}}\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}. (91)

Inequality (91) also holds when μi∈{1,(d−1)​(k−1)}\mu_{i}\in\{1,(d-1)(k-1)\}. Thus, from the two cases above, Theorem 3.8 (2) holds. ∎

9. Proof of Theorem 3.10

The spectral gap estimate for the adjacency matrix of an RSBM is known from [17]. We recall this result below and then prove Theorem 3.10 using the spectral relation between AA and B~\widetilde{B} established in Lemma 4.1.

Lemma 9.1.

Let AA be the adjacency matrix of an (n,d1,d2)(n,d_{1},d_{2})-regular stochastic block model. Then with high probability, (d1+d2),(d1−d2)(d_{1}+d_{2}),(d_{1}-d_{2}) are two eigenvalues of AA with multiplicity one. Moreover, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, all eigenvalues λ∉{d1+d2,d1−d2}\lambda\notin\{d_{1}+d_{2},d_{1}-d_{2}\} satisfy

limn→∞ℙ⁡(|λ|≤2​d1+d2−1+ε)=1.\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(|\lambda|\leq 2\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}+\varepsilon\right)=1. (92)
Proof.

This is shown in [16, Section 4] by using the result of the spectral gap of random lifts from [12, Corollary 24], and contiguity of the permutation model and the configuration model of regular graphs from [32, Theorem 1.3]. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.10.

Since an (n,d1,d2)(n,d_{1},d_{2})-regular stochastic block model is a (d1+d2)(d_{1}+d_{2})-regular graph, the first statement follows from Lemma 4.1 directly.

For the second statement, let AA be the adjacency matrix of an (n,d1,d2)(n,d_{1},d_{2}) regular stochastic block model. Since d1−d2d_{1}-d_{2} is an eigenvalue for AA with associated eigenvector σ\sigma, from Lemma 4.1, there are two eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} satisfying

μ2−(d1−d2)​μ+(d1+d2−1)=0.\displaystyle\mu^{2}-(d_{1}-d_{2})\mu+(d_{1}+d_{2}-1)=0. (93)

When (d1−d2)2>4​(d1+d2−1)(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}>4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1), the two eigenvalues are real, and the second statement holds.

We now show the third statement. From Lemma 9.1, since d1+d2,d1−d2d_{1}+d_{2},d_{1}-d_{2} are two eigenvalues of AA with multiplicity one with high probability, Lemma 4.1 shows that d1+d2−1,1,μ2,μ2′d_{1}+d_{2}-1,1,\mu_{2},\mu_{2}^{\prime} are four real eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} with multiplicity one with high probability when (d1−d2)2>4​(d1+d2−1)(d_{1}-d_{2})^{2}>4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1). Let λ\lambda be an eigenvalue of AA with λ∉{d1+d2,d1−d2}\lambda\not\in\{d_{1}+d_{2},d_{1}-d_{2}\}. With Lemma 4.1, |λ|≤2​d1+d2−1+ε|\lambda|\leq 2\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}+\varepsilon with high probability, and the corresponding two eigenvalues μ,μ′\mu,\mu^{\prime} of B~\tilde{B} satisfies

x2−λ​x+(d1+d2−1)=0.\displaystyle x^{2}-\lambda x+(d_{1}+d_{2}-1)=0. (94)

We consider two cases:

  1. (1)

    If |λ|≤2​d1+d2−1|\lambda|\leq 2\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}, then the associated two eigenvalues have |μ|=|μ′|=d1+d2−1|\mu|=|\mu^{\prime}|=\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}.

  2. (2)

    If |λ|∈[2​d1+d2−1,2​d1+d2−1+ε]|\lambda|\in[2\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1},2\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}+\varepsilon], μ,μ′\mu,\mu^{\prime} are real and

    μ,μ′=λ±λ2−4​(d1+d2−1)2.\displaystyle\mu,\mu^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda\pm\sqrt{\lambda^{2}-4(d_{1}+d_{2}-1)}}{2}. (95)

    We have for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), with high probability,

    |μ−d1+d2−1|,|μ′−d1+d2−1|≤C​ε\displaystyle|\mu-\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}|,|\mu^{\prime}-\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}|\leq C\sqrt{\varepsilon} (96)

    for a constant CC depending only on (d1+d2−1)(d_{1}+d_{2}-1).

Therefore, all eigenvalues λ∉\lambda\not\in{d1+d2−1,1,μ2,μ2′}\{d_{1}+d_{2}-1,1,\mu_{2},\mu_{2}^{\prime}\} are within o⁡(1)o(1) distance from the circle of radius d1+d2−1\sqrt{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}. This completes the proof of Theorem 3.10. ∎

10. Erdős-Rényi graphs

Studying bulk non-backtracking eigenvectors for G⁡(n,p)G(n,p) is an interesting open problem. Previously, using the fact that when n​p=ω⁡(log⁡n)np=\omega(\log n) the degrees in G⁡(n,p)G(n,p) are concentrated around n​pnp, [56, 22] studied the eigenvalues of B~\tilde{B} by approximating the degree matrix DD with (n​p)​In(np)I_{n}, and analyzed a perturbed quadratic equation from the Ihara-Bass formula. However, it is not clear to us how to generalize this partial de-randomization argument introduced in [56] to study eigenvector delocalization. We conjecture that non-backtracking eigenvector delocalization holds when n​p=ω⁡(log⁡n)np=\omega(\log n) and does not hold for n​p=o⁡(log⁡n)np=o(\log n), similar to the results established for the adjacency matrix [55, 25, 34, 3, 2, 4]. See Figure 6 for simulation results.
